The Spanish toothcarp Aphanius iberus is a small cyprinodontiform fish endemic to coastal and inland brackish habitats of the Iberian Peninsula. Field surveys across its fragmented range consistently report that the largest individuals attain an ultimate total length of 5.5 centimeters [Li = 5.5 centimeters], a modest size that places it among the smaller representatives of the genus. This species exhibits pronounced sexual dimorphism, with males displaying more vivid pigmentation during the breeding season. Its life history is tightly constrained by the ephemeral and often hypersaline nature of its preferred environments. Adult body mass is correspondingly low, with the ultimate wet weight reaching approximately 2.3 grams [Wwi = approximately 2.3 grams] in gravid females, a figure derived from length-mass regressions and confirmed by direct weighing of preserved museum specimens. Such a low body mass reflects the stringent energetic constraints imposed by intermittent lagoon systems where productivity fluctuates dramatically with seasonal rainfall patterns. The species is iteroparous and capable of multiple spawning events within a single warm season, an adaptation that enhances reproductive assurance in unpredictable settings.

Juveniles of Aphanius iberus undergo rapid early growth to escape the size-selective predation pressure exerted by co-occurring predatory invertebrates and fishes. The wet weight at birth, representing the mass of the newly hatched yolk-sac larva immediately following chorion rupture, is approximately 0.0018 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.0018 grams]. This remarkably low initial mass derives from the small egg diameter typical of the species, which ranges between 0.75 and 1.75 millimeters. The yolk-sac larva is entirely lecithotrophic for the first several days, relying exclusively on its endogenous reserves while completing organogenesis. At a stable water temperature of 22 °C [T = 22 °C], the age at birth, defined as the interval between oviposition and successful eclosion from the chorion, lasts approximately 8 days [ab = approximately 8 days]. Hatching success in captivity under these thermal conditions exceeds seventy percent when salinity is maintained between ten and fifteen parts per thousand, conditions that mimic the fish's natural nursery habitat. The rapid absorption of yolk during this period underscores the importance of warm temperatures for accelerating developmental rates in this thermophilic species.

Reproductive allocation in Aphanius iberus reflects a strategy that balances fecundity against the constraints of small body size and short generation time. Under laboratory conditions maintained at a constant 22 °C [T = 22 °C], females produce approximately 1 to 3 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = approximately 1 to 3 eggs per clutch] and, during the peak of the spawning season, can deposit over 2.5 clutches per day [F_R_i = over 2.5 clutches per day]. The maximum daily reproduction rate thereby corresponds to approximately 2.46 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 2.46 eggs per day], one of the highest values recorded among small cyprinodontids, a rate facilitated by the continuous availability of appropriate submerged vegetation for oviposition. The total length at puberty, marking the size at which individuals first display secondary sexual characteristics and functional gonads, is 2.5 centimeters [Lp = 2.5 centimeters]. Individuals reach this size threshold remarkably quickly, typically within two months of hatching under optimal growing conditions. Such early maturation is a classic correlate of an opportunistic life-history strategy common in species inhabiting unpredictable environments.

Longevity data for Aphanius iberus indicate a comparatively brief lifespan relative to larger cyprinodontids, consistent with its rapid maturation and high investment in early reproduction. In wild populations inhabiting the stable coastal lagoons of the Ebro Delta, the maximum recorded lifespan has been estimated at approximately 1.4 years [am = approximately 1.4 years] when individuals experience persistent temperatures averaging 22 °C [T = 22 °C]. This figure is based on otolith increment analysis of the oldest specimens collected during seasonal mark-recapture studies. Observations from captive colonies corroborate this pattern, with most individuals succumbing to senescent decline shortly after the conclusion of their second reproductive summer. The short lifespan is intimately linked to a semelparous-like reproductive exhaustion in males, who exhibit pronounced physical deterioration following sustained territorial defense and courtship. Females, while typically surviving slightly longer, also show a pronounced drop in spawning frequency after reaching one year of age, suggesting a steep actuarial senescence curve.

Comparative ecophysiological studies place Aphanius iberus among the most thermally tolerant yet short-lived members of its family in the western Palearctic. Its basal metabolic rate at the preferred thermal range of 22 °C [T = 22 °C] is elevated relative to that of non-cyprinodontid fishes of comparable adult size, reaching an adult length of 5.5 centimeters [Li = 5.5 centimeters], reflecting its active foraging habit and continuous reproductive output. The low ultimate wet weight of Aphanius iberus, approximately 2.3 grams [Wwi = approximately 2.3 grams], falls at the lower end of values reported for the genus, suggesting a selective pressure favoring small body size in ephemeral habitats. The age at birth of approximately 8 days [ab = approximately 8 days] is brief enough to allow multiple generations within a single favorable season, while the total length at puberty of 2.5 centimeters [Lp = 2.5 centimeters] is achieved before the onset of the summer dry period in many coastal marshes at a temperature of 22 °C [T = 22 °C]. Maximum lifespan of approximately 1.4 years [am = approximately 1.4 years] overlaps with a single annual hydrologic cycle in temporary wetlands, reinforcing the interpretation that Aphanius iberus is a textbook example of an opportunistic, r-selected fish species at a temperature of 22 °C [T = 22 °C].
